title: Blind to Change

paragraphs.text: Picture the following and prepare to be amazed. You’re walking across a college campus when a stranger asks you for directions. While you’re talking to him, two men pass between you carrying a wooden door. You feel a moment’s irritation, but you carry on describing the route. When you’ve finished, you’re told you’ve just taken part in a psychology experiment. ‘Did you notice anything after the two men passed with the door?’ the stranger asks. ‘No,’ you reply uneasily. He explains that the man who initially approached you walked off behind the door leaving him in his place. The first man now rejoins you. Comparing them, you notice that they are of different height and build and are dressed very differently.

Daniel Simons of Harvard University found that 50% of participants missed the substitution because of what is called ‘change blindness’. When considered with a large number of recent experimental results, this phenomenon suggests we ‘see’ far less than we think we do. Rather than logging every detail of the visual scene, says Simons, we are actually highly selective. Our impression of seeing everything is just that. In fact, we extract a few details and rely on memory, or even our imagination, for the rest.

Until recently, researchers thought that seeing involved making pictures in the brain. By building detailed internal representations of the world, and comparing them over time, we could spot any changes. Then in Consciousness Explained, the philosopher Daniel Dennett claimed that our brains hold only a few salient details about the world – and that is why we are able to operate successfully.

Elaborating pictures in short-term memory, Dennett said, would use valuable computing power. Rather, we log what has changed and assume the rest has stayed the same. Inevitably, we miss a few details. Experimenters had shown that we ignore things in the visual field if they appear insignificant – a repeated word or line on a page of text, for instance. But not even Dennett realised quite how little we really do ‘see’.

A year later, John Grimes of the University of Illinois caused a stir when he described how people who were shown computer-generated pictures of a natural scene were blind to changes that were made while the eye was, for example, scanning a scene or blinking. Dennett was delighted: ‘I wish in retrospect that I’d been more daring, since the effects are stronger than I claimed.’

Since then, it has been found that our eyes needn’t be moving to be fooled. A typical lab demonstration might show a picture on a computer screen of, say, a couple dining on a terrace. The picture would disappear, replaced momentarily by a blank screen, before reappearing significantly altered by the raising of a railing behind the couple, perhaps.

Many people search the screen for up to a minute before they see the change. A few never do. It’s unnerving. But to some extent ‘change blindness’ is artificial because in real life there tends to be a visible movement that signals the change. But not always. As Simons points out, ‘We all know the experience of not noticing a traffic signal change because we had briefly looked away. “Inattentional blindness” means that if you are not paying attention to some feature of a scene, you won’t see it.’

Last year, Simons showed people a videotape of a basketball game and asked them to count the passes made by one team. After 45 seconds, a man dressed in a gorilla suit walked slowly across behind the players. Forty per cent failed to notice him. When the tape was replayed, and they were simply asked to watch it, they saw him easily. Some refused to believe it was the same tape.

Now imagine that the viewers had been driving a car, and the gorilla-man had been a pedestrian. According to some estimates, nearly half of all fatal motor vehicle accidents in the US can be attributed to driver error, including lapses in attention. It is more than just academic interest that has made both forms of cognitive error hot research topics.

Such errors raise important questions: how can we reconcile these gross lapses with our subjective experience of having continuous access to a rich visual scene? Last year, Stephen Kosslyn of Harvard University showed that envisaging a scene activates parts of the visual cortex in the same way as seeing it. He says that this supports the idea that we take in just what information we consider important, and fill in the gaps where mere details are less important. ‘The illusion that we see “everything” is partly a result of filling in the gaps using memory,’ he says. ‘Such memories can be based on beliefs and expectations.’

Ronald Rensink of the University of British Columbia, Canada, believes our impression of a rich visual world comes from our building internal representations. According to him, the brain first constructs a temporary layout of the visual scene. Then our attention applies a higher level of resolution to the scene. ‘What attention does,’ he explains, ‘is to stabilise these representations so that they form an individual object. The moment attention is released, they dissolve back into the volatile, unresolved landscape.’

But while Rensink or Kosslyn argue for some role for internal images or memory, others argue that we can get the impression of visual richness without holding any of the richness in our heads. Kevin O’Regan, an experimental psychologist, argues that we hold no picture of the visual world in our brains. Instead, we refer back to the external visual world as different aspects of a scene become important.

According to O’Regan, our sense of controlling what we see is also illusory. ‘We think that when something flickers outside the window, we decide to look,’ says Susan Blackmore of the University of the West of England, a supporter of O’Regan’s. ‘In fact,’ she says, ‘we are at the mercy of our change detection mechanisms, which automatically drag our attention here, there and everywhere.’
